g11-economics-ue7-t1.overview: Ethiopia's current development strategy treats agriculture as the leading sector of the economy. This lesson covers the uni-modal and bi-modal agricultural strategies, the specific agricultural policies of the Imperial, Derg and post-1991 governments, and the problems of the sector together with their remedies.
objectives: Define and compare the uni-modal and bi-modal agricultural strategies
Explain why the agricultural sector is viewed as the leading sector in Ethiopia's strategy of development
Analyze the agricultural policies and strategies of the Imperial regime, the Derg and the post-1991 governments
Classify the problems of the agricultural sector as natural or human-made
Evaluate the remedies proposed to raise agricultural productivity in Ethiopia
g11-economics-ue7-t1.simple: Agriculture is the mainstay of the Ethiopian economy, so the current strategy makes it the leading sector through ADLI, Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization. Two general approaches exist. The uni-modal strategy transforms agriculture by intensifying small-scale peasant farms with divisible innovations such as improved seeds and fertilizer, as in Japan and China. The bi-modal strategy combines peasant intensification with commercialization on large farms, as in Mexico and Colombia. Each era applied its own policies. The Imperial regime tried large-scale mechanized commercial farms and package projects; the Derg nationalized land and collectivized peasants; the post-1991 government liberalized markets and adopted ADLI, PADETES, SDPRP, PASDEP and the growth and transformation plans. The main problems are drought, land fragmentation, poor infrastructure and backward technology, addressed through irrigation, afforestation, secure land rights and stronger extension services.
g11-economics-ue7-t1.detailed:
Why agriculture is the leading sector. Western economies gave priority to the industrial sector on the assumption that it has the greatest potential to adopt technology and to create forward and backward linkages with other sectors. Since the 1970s, however, development economists have come to realize that the agricultural sector is a leading and dynamic sector and that, without its development, the growth of the industrial sector will become weak. Agriculture is the mainstay of the Ethiopian economy, and this is the approach of the current Ethiopian strategy of development. The policies applied include market liberalization, structural adjustment, Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI), the Sustainable Development and Poverty Reduction Program (SDPRP), Participatory and Accelerated Sustainable Development to Eradicate Poverty (PASDEP), the successive Growth and Transformation Plans I and II, and the current ten years Prosperity Plan. Since 1991 all subsidies and price support measures to agriculture were abolished, and a structural adjustment program reduced the role of government while increasing the role of demand and supply forces in allocating resources. All these interventions aim to increase agricultural productivity and production, which in turn reduces poverty and food insecurity.

The uni-modal agricultural strategy. The uni-modal strategy achieves agricultural transformation through intensification of small-scale peasant farms. It is based on the concept that peasants are not separated from their means of production and retain a degree of control over land and family labor, as in Japan, Thailand and China. Its central element is the development and diffusion of highly divisible innovations, such as improved seeds and fertilizers that promote output expansion within the existing small-size holdings. It is a pro-poor growth strategy that enhances smallholders' access to modern inputs on revolving-credit bases and focuses on food crops to ensure food security. Its advantages are that it protects the peasant group from eviction, reduces poverty in the rural economy, gives individual peasants access to modern technologies, reduces outgoing migration from rural areas and creates political support for the government. Its limitations are its focus on food crops rather than high-value market products, its inability to improve knowledge of market information and weather conditions, poor infrastructure caused by fragmented settlement patterns, difficulty of employing large-scale inputs on small holdings, and the absence of controls against rising input prices.

The bi-modal agricultural strategy. The bi-modal strategy advocates both the intensification of small peasant farms and commercialization. It is based on a dualistic structure of farm units, as in Mexico and Colombia, which proposes that commercialization and commoditization inevitably generate differentiation in agrarian societies, setting rural producers apart into agricultural capitalists and landless agricultural employees. Its characteristics are support for a strong principal commercial sector, allowing entrepreneurial individuals to accumulate land, and supporting differentiation between those who invest more in farming and those who develop business. Its advantages are that it supports individual rights to acquire land, invites more capital and technology investment, promotes large-scale diversification and allows the transfer of technology. Its limitations are that it creates differentiation in rural society, lacks off-farm job opportunities, promotes the eviction of small peasants and deprives the majority of the rural population of land.

Pre-1974 policies and strategies. Under the Imperial regime the priority focus was given to industry, minerals and electric power development, with only some attention to agriculture. Targets were set for marketable products such as cereals, cotton, cattle and coffee, to be achieved through land reform, the introduction of tools and machinery with elementary training of producers, and raising per capita income to transform the subsistence economy into a monetized economy. The land reform policy was completely ignored, which basically accounted for the failure of the plan. The third five-year plan then outlined two approaches. The Large-Scale Mechanized Commercial Farm (LSMCF) aimed to facilitate agricultural exports and create employment, using modern technology, machinery, fertilizers and hired labor; incentives included credit arrangements, tax holidays for the first five years for investments in excess of 200,000 Birr, low land use fees, tax-free import of heavy machinery and the possibility of remitting profits. Yet the results were too small to achieve the given incentives: foreign-owned plantations accounted for almost 5% of total agricultural output and 3% of the total cultivated area, and were nationalized and converted into state farms in 1975. The package projects aimed to repeat the success of the Green Revolution of India, which used large-scale high-yield variety (HYV) seeds. Comprehensive Package Projects supplied chemicals, fertilizers, improved seeds, farm tools, credit, pesticides and know-how to raise peasant living standards and create labor-intensive employment; the Chilalo Agricultural Development Unit (CADU), the Welayita Agricultural Development Unit (WADU) and the Adaa District Development Package Project (ADDP) increased income, productivity and the adoption of modern inputs, but tenant eviction increased and the huge cost made duplication impossible. The cheaper minimum package program was launched over wider areas to raise smallholder production quickly with a minimum reliance on scarce resources, but the small resources allocated made it unsuccessful.

Policies during the Derg regime (1974-1991). The Derg changed the strategy to a centrally planned economy with industry-led development. Rural land and other productive assets were nationalized and distributed among farmers, commercial farms were put under government control, land tenancy was abolished, and large collectivization programs were promoted through resettlement and villagization. The package projects continued: CADU became the Arsi Rural Development Unit (ARDU), then the Bale-Arsi Rural Development Unit (BARDU), thinning resources over wide areas, and finally all became Peasant Agricultural Development Extension Projects (PADEP). In general, agricultural policy was characterized by nationalization of all private and commercial farms, prohibition of private investment, involuntary collectivization into peasant associations and producers' and service cooperatives, forced villagization and settlements, government control of virtually all input and output markets, forced food-grain quota deliveries at predetermined low prices, and restriction of the movement of agricultural outputs. These improper government interventions were the primary reason for the lack of success of the agricultural sector and the national economy in general.

Post-1991 policies and strategies. The 1991 economic policy document of the Transitional Government declared collectivization and villagization undesirable and liberalized agricultural markets. The government adopted ADLI in 1994, which revolves around enhancing the productivity of smallholder agriculture and industrialization based on domestic raw materials using labor-intensive technology; its essence is the belief that agriculture can serve as the driving force for the rest of the economy through its internal forward and backward linkages with industry. The Participatory Demonstration and Training Extension System (PADETES), launched in 1994/95, delivered packages of fertilizer, improved seed and credit, together with information on better agricultural practices, to the vast majority of smallholders, yet average agricultural output still failed to sustain the high population growth. The Sustainable Development and Poverty Reduction Program (SDPRP) of 2002 was the first full Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP) of Ethiopia; it strengthened agricultural extension, trained extension agents through TVET and farmers through Farmers Training Centers, promoted water harvesting and irrigation, improved marketing opportunities, restructured peasant cooperatives and supported micro-financing institutions. However, heavy dependence on the amount and timing of rainfall makes output fluctuate and productivity show no significant improvement. Under PASDEP, large-scale commercial agriculture was emphasized with instruments such as farm-to-market roads, agricultural credit markets, specialized extension services for different agricultural zones, national business plans and tailored packages for specialized export crops such as spices, cut flowers, fruits and vegetables, area irrigation through multi-purpose dams, measures to improve land tenure security, and fertilizer and seed reforms. The later strategies are the successive growth and transformation plans and, most recently, priorities of small and large-scale irrigation development, financing agricultural inputs, mechanization, post-harvest loss reduction, a research-based food security system and natural resource management, with the Home-Grown Economic Reform Agenda looking to agro-processing as one engine of future growth.

Problems and remedies of the agricultural sector. The natural problems relate to recurrent drought: almost all highland farming and livestock practices depend on rainfall, and its variability in time and amount affects crop production and livestock rearing, with millions of cattle dying. The human-made problems include land fragmentation as average landholdings shrink, making over-cultivation inevitable; lack of infrastructure, since about 75% of rural household farms are located far from transportation and communication lines, blocking access to markets and price information; lack of credit facilities, though reforms have now opened access to micro-finance loans; lack of effective land ownership entitlement, which causes poor work attitudes and improper use of resources; erosion and land degradation, which contribute to the recurrence of drought; traditional practices that misuse work time and keep livestock unscientifically; the use of backward technology; and inadequate rural markets. Possible remedies are promoting irrigation from local streams and lakes, storing rainwater in shade to reduce evaporation, expanding afforestation and reforestation through a structured and financed agency, producing drought-resistant crops in drought-prone areas, pursuing effective land ownership rights so farmers develop long-term commitments, promoting extension services with consistent capacity building, running committed literacy campaigns so farmers understand price and farm-technique information, and developing infrastructure facilities.

keyTerms.def: A strategy by which agricultural transformation is achieved through intensification of small-scale peasant farms, as in Japan, Thailand and China.
A strategy advocating both the intensification of small peasant farms and commercialization, based on a dualistic farm structure, as in Mexico and Colombia.
Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization, adopted in 1994; it enhances smallholder productivity and industrializes using domestic raw materials and labor-intensive technology.
The Participatory Demonstration and Training Extension System launched in 1994/95, delivering packages of fertilizer, improved seed and credit to most smallholders.
Large-Scale Mechanized Commercial Farm of the Imperial era, meant to facilitate exports and employment; it reached only about 5% of agricultural output and 3% of cultivated area.
An Imperial-era project supplying chemicals, fertilizers, improved seeds, tools, credit, pesticides and know-how; CADU, WADU and ADDP were examples.
A cheaper, wide-area program designed to raise smallholder production and income quickly with minimum reliance on scarce resources; it failed due to small allocations.
Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper; Ethiopia's first full PRSP was the Sustainable Development and Poverty Reduction Program (SDPRP) launched in 2002.

workedExamples.problem: In total agricultural output of 3,000 million Birr, LSMCF plantations accounted for about 5% of output and 3% of cultivated area. What value did commercial farms produce, and what does this show about the incentives given?
workedExamples.given: Total agricultural output = 3,000 million Birr; LSMCF share = 5%.
workedExamples.formula: LSMCF output = share x total output.
workedExamples.calculation: 150 million Birr came from farms that received tax holidays, cheap land and tax-free machinery imports.
workedExamples.answer: About 150 million Birr. The results were too small to achieve the given incentives, showing the failure of the LSMCF path.

workedExamples.problem: A government wants a pro-poor agricultural policy that protects peasants from eviction and ensures food security. Which strategy fits, and what costs does it accept?
workedExamples.given: Goals: protect smallholders, food security; small landholdings dominate.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: match goals to strategy characteristics.
workedExamples.substitution: The uni-modal strategy is pro-poor and focuses on food crops within small holdings; the bi-modal strategy promotes differentiation and eviction.
workedExamples.calculation: The uni-modal strategy meets the goals, but accepts the limits of food-crop focus, small plots and weak market information.
workedExamples.answer: The uni-modal strategy, which is Ethiopia-like in its protection of peasants, at the cost of slower high-value commercialization.

workedExamples.problem: A peasant delivers food grain to a government store at a predetermined low price while input and output markets are state controlled. Identify the era and the economic effect.
workedExamples.given: Forced quota deliveries at low prices; government control of markets.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: low controlled prices and restricted markets reduce producer incentives.
workedExamples.substitution: The features match the Derg agricultural policies of 1974-1991.
workedExamples.calculation: When farmers receive low fixed prices and cannot move output, supply incentives fall, so output and productivity decline.
workedExamples.answer: The Derg era; improper interventions were the primary reason for the sector's lack of success.

workedExamples.problem: In a zone with 800 rural household farms, about 75% are located far from transportation and communication lines. How many farms are far from markets, and why does this matter economically?
workedExamples.given: Total farms = 800; share far from transport lines = 75%.
workedExamples.calculation: 600 farms cannot access proper markets or price information, so farmers receive lower farm-gate prices and fewer inputs reach them.
workedExamples.answer: About 600 farms; poor transport access prevents proper market participation and lowers rural income.

commonMistakes: Saying the current Ethiopian strategy is industry-led, when it is agriculture-led under ADLI.
Confusing the uni-modal strategy with the bi-modal strategy; only the bi-modal one adds large-scale commercialization.
Believing the Imperial regime gave priority to agriculture, when industry, minerals and electric power came first.
Assuming package projects were cheap and easy to duplicate, when their huge cost forced the shift to the minimum package program.
Thinking the Derg liberalized agriculture, when it controlled markets and imposed forced quotas at low prices.
Claiming all agricultural problems are natural, when land fragmentation, backward technology and poor infrastructure are human-made.
Forgetting that post-1991 reforms abolished subsidies and price supports rather than increasing them.
applications: Explaining why grain prices rose sharply in a drought year: rain-fed farming makes output fluctuate with rainfall.
Proposing small-scale irrigation from a local stream in your kebele to reduce dependence on rain-fed farming.
Using a literacy campaign to help farmers in your area read price and farm-technique information.
Observing how repeated inheritance has fragmented family plots into smaller parcels over time.
Understanding how micro-finance loans can now help a rural family buy fertilizer and improved seed.
Linking agro-processing under the Home-Grown Economic Reform Agenda to higher income for crop growers.
g11-economics-ue7-t1.summary: Ethiopia's strategy places agriculture first: the uni-modal path intensifies small peasant farms, while the bi-modal path adds commercialization, each with its own advantages and limitations. Policies evolved from the Imperial LSMCF and package projects, through Derg nationalization, quotas and collectivization, to post-1991 liberalization with ADLI, PADETES, SDPRP, PASDEP and the growth and transformation plans. The sector still suffers from drought, fragmentation, weak infrastructure, credit and land tenure gaps and backward technology, which remedies such as irrigation, afforestation, secure land rights, literacy and extension services try to address.

questions.q: Since the 1970s, development economists have argued that:
options: the agricultural sector needs to be the leading and dynamic sector
agriculture is purely passive in development
questions.explanation: Since the 1970s economists realized agriculture must be seen as a leading sector, and without it industrial growth becomes weak.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of the uni-modal agricultural strategy?
options: Diffusion of highly divisible innovations within small holdings
questions.explanation: The uni-modal strategy develops and diffuses highly divisible innovations that expand output within small-size holdings.

questions.q: A limitation of the bi-modal strategy is that it:
options: focuses too much on food crops
promotes the eviction of small peasants and deprives the majority of land
questions.explanation: The bi-modal strategy promotes eviction of small peasants, creates differentiation and deprives most of the rural population of land.

questions.q: The LSMCF path accounted for almost 5% of total agricultural output and 3% of cultivated area.
questions.explanation: Despite the incentives given, LSMCF results were too small: about 5% of output and 3% of cultivated area.

questions.q: The minimum package program succeeded because it was given abundant resources.
questions.explanation: The small amount of resources allocated made the minimum package projects unsuccessful.

questions.q: Name, in full, the strategy the Ethiopian government adopted in 1994 to make agriculture the driving force of the economy.
questions.answer: agricultural development-led industrialization|agricultural development led industrialization|adli
questions.explanation: ADLI, Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization, was adopted in 1994.

questions.q: Give one reason the comprehensive package projects could not be duplicated in other areas of the country.
questions.answer: huge cost|their high cost was too large|eviction of tenants
questions.explanation: The huge cost of the projects, and adverse effects like increased tenant eviction, made duplication too difficult.

questions.q: During the Derg regime, agricultural policy included all of the following EXCEPT:
options: forced quota deliveries at low prices
questions.explanation: The Derg controlled markets and restricted output movement; liberalization came only after 1991.

questions.q: About what share of Ethiopian rural household farms are far from transportation and communication lines, and what is one consequence?
questions.explanation: About 75% of rural household farms are far from such lines, preventing access to proper markets and price information.

questions.q: Order these agricultural strategies from first to last adopted.
questions.explanation: The order is ADLI (1994), PADETES (1994/95), SDPRP (2002), then PASDEP and the later growth and transformation plans.

questions.q: Name one human-made problem of the agricultural sector.
questions.answer: land fragmentation|lack of infrastructure|lack of credit|erosion|backward technology|inadequate rural markets|poor work attitudes
questions.explanation: Human-made problems include land fragmentation, lack of infrastructure, lack of credit, erosion, traditional practices and backward technology.

questions.q: Which remedy attacks drought most directly at its source of dependence?
options: Producing drought-resistant crops and promoting irrigation
questions.explanation: Remedies reduce dependence on rain-fed farming through irrigation, water storage and drought-resistant crops.

g11-economics-ue7-t2.overview: Industrialization is the surest path out of poverty, but it demands careful policy management. This lesson traces Ethiopian industrial policy from the import-substitution of the Imperial regime, through Derg nationalization, to the post-1991 Industrial Development Strategy and industrial parks, and then analyzes the sector's problems and remedies.
objectives: Explain why industrialization is considered essential for socioeconomic transformation
Analyze industrial policy under the Imperial regime, the Derg and the post-1991 government
Describe the 2003 Industrial Development Strategy and the principles of industrial park development
Classify the problems of the industrial sector as finance, marketing, technological or input-related
Evaluate the remedies needed to create a conducive business environment for the private sector
g11-economics-ue7-t2.simple: Hardly any society has achieved socioeconomic transformation without industrialization; the success of Asian economies shows it is the surest way to reduce poverty. The Imperial regime, from the mid-1950s, promoted import-substituting light industries with tariffs, fiscal incentives and credit, financed mostly by foreign investment, leaving a weak dual industrial base. The Derg nationalized most medium- and large-scale enterprises, restricted private investment, imposed price controls and ran the zemecha production campaign. After 1991 the government first promoted exports in 1998, then adopted a comprehensive Industrial Development Strategy in 2002/03, based on ADLI, export-led and labor-intensive growth, private sector leadership and priority sectors like textiles, leather, agro-processing and construction. Industrial parks attract investment, create jobs and link Ethiopia to global value chains. Main problems are lack of finance, weak markets, inappropriate technology and costly inputs.
g11-economics-ue7-t2.detailed:
Why industrialization matters. Modern economic history shows that the socioeconomic transformation of a society can rarely be achieved without industrialization. The astounding success of several Asian economies over the past half-century proves that it is the surest way to reduce poverty. Yet industrialization is not a structural inevitability: it requires careful management of policy options and consistent monitoring of sectoral dynamics.

The Imperial regime (pre-1974). A conscious move to stimulate industrial growth began in the mid-1950s. The plan aimed to develop import-substituting light industries producing consumer goods for the domestic market, with foreign direct private investment playing the leading financing role. Incentives included protection of domestic industry through high tariffs and bans on certain imports, fiscal incentives and the provision of credit. The government was also to provide infrastructure, human resource development and direct investment in high-capital sectors such as oil refinery, cement, sugar and textiles. The philosophy favored the market and the private sector, but in practice the incentive structure was biased toward import-substituting, larger, capital-intensive and foreign-dominated activities. By the end of the plan period the industrial base remained weak and dual: a rudimentary small-scale and handicraft sub-sector and a modern medium- and large-scale sub-sector, each contributing about half of manufacturing value added, with the modern sector (ten or more employees using power-driven machinery) predominantly foreign owned.

The Derg regime (1974-1991). The military government nationalized most MLSM enterprises and reorganized them under state corporations, declaring a socialist economic policy. Private investment was restricted so it could not exceed half a million Birr (about a quarter of a million US dollars), and entrepreneurs could participate in only one venture. Wide-ranging price controls were instituted, the labor market was highly regulated, and imports faced quantitative restrictions and higher tariffs. Manufacturing declined sharply in the first years after the revolution; in 1977/78 the successive production campaign known locally as zemecha partly reversed the decline by raising capacity utilization. The government had no industrial policy as such until the mid-1980s, when the plan promoted import-substituting, labor-intensive industries and treated public investment as the main mechanism of industrialization. In March 1990 the regime adopted a mixed economic policy, but it came too late and collapsed with the regime change in May 1991.

The post-1991 Industrial Development Strategy. In 1998 the government adopted an export promotion strategy to address poor export diversification, promoting high-value agricultural exports such as horticulture products and meat and labor-intensive manufactures such as clothing, textiles, and leather and leather products; it was relatively narrow. A comprehensive Industrial Development Strategy (IDS) was formulated in 2002/03, based on ADLI. It emphasized export-led industrialization focused on labor-intensive industries, infrastructure to support rapid economic growth, and small enterprises for massive job creation and poverty reduction. Its fundamental principles are considering the private sector as the engine of industrial development, implementing ADLI and export-led industrialization, focusing on labor-intensive industry, effective domestic-foreign investment partnership, a leading managerial role for the government, and active participation of the public. Priority sectors for direct government support were declared: textile and garment, meat, leather and leather products, other agro-processing industries such as sugar and sugar-related industries, the construction industry, and the micro and small enterprises (MSEs). Distinguishing rent-seeking from developmental capitalists, the strategy argues for a strong state that is not merely a facilitator but also a leader, inspired by the East Asian idea of the developmental state: it promotes the private sector by creating a conducive environment and provides direct support to selected sectors.

Industrial park development. Since the 1960s many countries have used industrial parks to promote industrialization and economic restructuring; by attracting labor- and capital-intensive domestic and foreign investment in manufacturing and service industries, parks increase jobs, wages and skills and link countries to global value chains, improving their position in the international division of labor. Ethiopian park development opens investment to domestic and foreign direct investment, builds state-of-the-art parks along key economic corridors connected to ports by road and electric-powered railway lines and close to large labor pools. Its principles are specialized (clustered) parks for economies of scale, export promotion through targeted incentives, sustainability through renewable energy and zero liquid discharge (ZLD) technology, vertical integration to enhance forward and backward linkages, and skills development for competitiveness. The parks have contributed significantly by creating employment, increasing government revenue and exports, diversifying industrial products, attracting foreign direct investment and foreign exchange, and introducing sophisticated technology to local manufacturing.

Problems of the industrial sector after 1991. Finance: agriculture has not generated the required surplus, industries are highly import-dependent and have not been net savers, so the low saving rate makes industrial investment difficult, and high collateral requirements of formal lenders aggravate the shortage. Marketing: weak domestic demand because the vast majority rely on subsistence agriculture so purchasing power is very low; lack of marketing information about local and export markets; strong competition from cheap imports; and a consumer bias against local products. Technology: lack of sufficient information on appropriate technology due to few local technological support institutions; technology not developed from available local raw materials, so limits linkage and worsens the foreign currency shortage, since the ratio of imported raw materials is too high, worst in basic iron and steel, motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers; and capital-intensive technology not recommended where unemployment is rising. Inputs: the high cost and shortage of foreign exchange for imported inputs causes raw material shortages, the second most serious problem after market problems; there are also policy problems and human-resource problems of lack of skilled manpower, industrial discipline and work ethics, which limit new investment and reduce the productive capacity of existing enterprises.

Possible remedies. Creating a conducive business environment for the private sector requires maintaining macroeconomic stability, building a functioning and well-regulated financial sector, creating dependable infrastructure services, developing skilled and effective human resources, creating an efficient civil service and legal framework, and developing industrial zones in major cities and towns with all required infrastructure. Improving the ease of doing business has been singled out as a priority reform: a better investment climate for local and foreign businesses will be critical as Ethiopia shifts from public-sector-led growth to private-sector-driven growth, and sustaining FDI inflows depends on removing key bottlenecks and widening investable opportunities.

keyTerms.def: An industrial strategy of producing consumer goods for the domestic market that were previously imported, used in the Imperial era.
Modern medium- and large-scale manufacturing that employs ten or more people and uses power-driven machinery; it was predominantly foreign owned before 1974.
The successive production campaign initiated in 1977/78 by the Derg to improve productivity mainly by increasing capacity utilization.
The comprehensive Industrial Development Strategy formulated in 2002/03, based on ADLI, export-led and labor-intensive industrialization.
A policy principle on the state-business relationship in which the state leads, coordinates and directly supports selected sectors, not merely facilitates.
A capitalist type the IDS says government should curtail, in contrast to developmental capitalists who invest productively.
A spatially concentrated zone that attracts domestic and foreign investment in manufacturing and services to link firms to global value chains.
Zero liquid discharge technology used in Ethiopian industrial parks to keep high environmental standards together with renewable energy.

workedExamples.problem: Capital-intensive technology is not recommended for Ethiopia where unemployment is rising, unlike labor-intensive technology. Explain the economic reason.
workedExamples.given: Rising unemployment; two possible technological choices.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: employment effect = jobs created per unit of investment.
workedExamples.substitution: Capital-intensive technology uses more machinery per worker, creating fewer jobs; labor-intensive production absorbs more of Ethiopia's abundant labor.
workedExamples.calculation: With idle labor abundant and capital scarce, labor-intensive industrialization raises employment and output per unit of scarce capital, which is why the IDS focused on it.
workedExamples.answer: Labor-intensive technology suits a labor-abundant, capital-scarce economy; capital-intensive technology would add few jobs and aggravate unemployment.

workedExamples.problem: The Derg capped private investment at half a million Birr (about a quarter of a million US dollars). What implicit exchange rate does this reveal, and what effect did the cap have?
workedExamples.given: Cap = 500,000 Birr; cap = about 250,000 US dollars.
workedExamples.formula: Exchange rate = birr cap / dollar cap.
workedExamples.calculation: At about 2 birr per dollar, the cap was small, so private enterprise could not grow beyond one modest venture, and manufacturing declined after nationalization.
workedExamples.answer: About 2 birr per dollar; the cap plus nationalization suppressed private industrial investment.

workedExamples.problem: If each half of the dual industrial structure contributed about half of manufacturing value added, what does this tell a planner about the modern MLSM sub-sector?
workedExamples.given: Rudimentary handicrafts and modern MLSM each contribute about 50% of value added.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: structure of value added shows the strength of the industrial base.
workedExamples.substitution: Modern power-driven industry supplies only half despite receiving the incentives.
workedExamples.calculation: Half the value added still comes from rudimentary handicrafts, so the modern sub-sector alone cannot drive transformation.
workedExamples.answer: The industrial base was weak and dual; the modern MLSM sector needed domestic roots to lift the whole sector.

workedExamples.problem: An Ethiopian steel mill imports most of its raw materials and faces a foreign currency shortage. Trace the chain of effects on its output and on new investment.
workedExamples.given: High import ratio; shortage of foreign exchange.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: imported input cost x availability governs capacity utilization.
workedExamples.substitution: Scarce foreign exchange plus costly inputs creates raw material shortage, the second most serious problem after marketing.
workedExamples.calculation: Raw material shortage cuts production of existing firms and signals high risk to investors, so new investment is also limited.
workedExamples.answer: Output falls first; then lack of skilled prospects and finance deters new industrial investment, deepening import dependence.

commonMistakes: Saying the Imperial regime pursued a socialist industrial policy, when it favored the market and private sector.
Believing the Derg had an industrial policy from the start, when it had none as such until the mid-1980s.
Thinking the 1998 export promotion strategy was comprehensive, when it was relatively narrow; the full IDS came in 2002/03.
Assuming the 2003 IDS ignored the private sector, when it declared it the engine of industrial development.
Attributing weak domestic industrial demand to high incomes, when subsistence agriculture keeps purchasing power very low.
Forgetting that marketing problems, not finance, are named the most serious problems of the sector.
Thinking industrial parks only serve foreign firms, when investment is open to domestic and foreign investors.
applications: Judging a new garment factory in a local industrial park as labor-intensive job creation for your woreda.
Noticing that many consumers prefer imported goods and why a consumer bias against local products weakens industry.
Relating a shortage of cement in the market to input and foreign-exchange constraints of local producers.
Seeing how TVET programs supply the skilled human resource the industrial sector lacks.
Explaining why the government builds roads and railway lines to ports before opening industrial parks.
g11-economics-ue7-t2.summary: Ethiopia's industrial policy moved from Imperial import substitution financed largely by foreign capital, through Derg nationalization, restriction and price controls, to the post-1991 export promotion and the 2002/03 Industrial Development Strategy built on ADLI, labor-intensive export industries, private-sector leadership and industrial parks. The sector still faces shortages of finance, weak domestic and export markets, imported input dependence and unsuitable technology. Remedies center on macroeconomic stability, better finance, infrastructure, human resources, industrial zones and improved ease of doing business.

questions.q: The Imperial-era industrial plan anticipated that investment capital for industry would come mainly from:
questions.explanation: The plan anticipated that foreign direct private investment would play the leading role in financing industrial capital.

questions.q: By the end of the Imperial plan period, manufacturing in Ethiopia had a dual structure in which each sub-sector contributed about:
questions.explanation: The rudimentary handicraft sub-sector and the modern MLSM sub-sector each contributed about half of manufacturing value added.

questions.q: The Derg government restricted private investment to not exceed half a million Birr and limited entrepreneurs to one venture.
questions.explanation: These were among the restrictions of the Derg's socialist economic policy.

questions.q: The Derg adopted a mixed economic policy in March 1990 and it produced visible industrial growth before 1991.
questions.explanation: The March 1990 mixed economic policy was too late and short-lived, bearing no fruit before the regime change of May 1991.

questions.explanation: The successive production campaign locally known as zemecha partly reversed the manufacturing decline.

g11-economics-ue7-t3.overview: The service sector spans trade, transport, banking, education, health, tourism and public administration. This lesson analyzes service-sector policies in Ethiopia from the Imperial era through the Derg to the post-1991 government, focusing on the education, health, transport and tourism sub-sectors, their problems and their remedies.
objectives: Describe the composition and categories of the service sector
Analyze education sector policies and strategies before 1974, during the Derg and after 1991
Outline the 1993 Health Policy and the goals of the Health Sector Development Plan
Explain the policy changes in the transport sector and the 2009 tourism development policy
Identify the problems of each service sub-sector and evaluate the proposed remedies
g11-economics-ue7-t3.simple: The service sector includes trade, hotels and restaurants, transport and communication, education, banking and insurance, public administration, health and other services. Services can be consumer-oriented, business-oriented or mixed, and physical, intellectual or aesthetic. In education, the Imperial government produced a review only in 1974; the Derg nationalized private schools and sent about 60,000 students and teachers to rural areas in the Zemecha; after 1991 the six-component ESDP expanded schools, teacher training and higher education. In health, the 1993 National Health Policy and the 20-year HSDP, now in its third phase, decentralized care and stressed prevention, accessibility and private and NGO participation. Transport was tightly controlled by Proclamation 107/1976 and deregulated by Proclamation 14/1992. Tourism, despite huge potential, grew only after better infrastructure and the 2009 tourism development policy.
g11-economics-ue7-t3.detailed:
What the service sector contains. The sector is composed of sub-sectors including trade, hotels and restaurants, transport and communication, education, banking and insurance, public administration and defense, health, and other services. Service industries can be classified as primarily consumer-oriented, providing a service directly to a consumer; primarily business-oriented, serving another business; or mixed, serving both. Their activities can also be described as physical, involving working with objects such as repairing cars, hairdressing and cooking; intellectual, providing education or training at university and vocational school levels; and aesthetic, providing artistic experiences such as museums, theater and musical performances.

Education sector policies. Before 1974 the government did not adopt a strategy, though it initiated a comprehensive study; the Education Sector Review (ESR) recommended attaining universal primary education, ruralizing curricula through informal training, equalizing educational opportunities and relating the whole system to national development, but it was not published until February 1974. After 1974 the military government dismantled the feudal socioeconomic structure: by early 1975 it closed Haile Selassie I University and senior secondary schools and deployed some 60,000 students and teachers to rural areas for the development through cooperation campaign known as Zemecha, and in 1975 it nationalized all private schools. Education for socialist consciousness, for production and for science and research were the objectives, while schools were spread more evenly toward neglected small towns and rural areas. Post-1991, the Education Sector Development Programme (ESDP) was launched with six components: primary education with construction, rehabilitation, curriculum revision, teacher upgrading and textbook supply; secondary education with expanded services and equipment; technical-vocational training; teacher training with in-service training, distance learning and school-management training; tertiary education to meet demand for teachers, engineers, health specialists and public administrators; and institutional capacity building of the Ministry and Regional Education Bureaus in planning, financial management, implementation, monitoring and evaluation.

Education problems and remedies. Problems include issues of relevance, quality, accessibility and equity; great disparity between relatively developed and undeveloped regions and between rural and urban areas; gender inequality; insufficient participation of stakeholders; inadequate facilities, insufficient teacher training, overcrowded classes and shortages of books and teaching materials; quality below the standard level; financial and resource constraints with few alternatives to the public budget; and a high drop-out rate. Remedies are to expand the participation of parents, teachers and communities in education affairs, provide adequate textbooks, materials and facilities, narrow the inequalities, inspect the private education sector to ensure minimum quality, certification standards and appropriate fees, and improve the quality of teachers through better training and motivation.

Health sector policies. The health care delivery system has historically been unable to respond quantitatively and qualitatively to the health needs of the people; definite policies were not formulated until 1963, and after the 1974 revolution the ten-year development plan of 1978 declared primary health care, although the system remained highly centralized with little public-private collaboration. The Transitional and Federal Government formulated the 1993 Health Policy and Strategy, aimed at reorganizing health services so they become more cost-effective and efficient and contribute more to socioeconomic development. The Health Sector Development Plan (HSDP), a comprehensive rolling 20-year plan formulated in 1997, is now in its third phase (HSDP III). The major goals of the health policy are decentralization of the health care system, development of preventive, facilitative and curative components, assurance of accessibility of health care for all segments of the population, and promotion of private-sector and NGO participation. The policy addresses communicable diseases, malnutrition, and maternal and child health; implementation is devolved largely to districts operating on block funding, and it stresses inter-sectoral collaboration in family planning, food and nutrition policy, and provision of safe and adequate water. Major strategy components are preventive and curative services, rehabilitative care, drugs and medical supplies, health information and documentation, organization and management, human resource development, research and development, and financing. Significant diseases addressed include COVID-19, HIV/AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis. Problems are limited physical access and absent facilities, uneven distribution across regions, inadequate budget and weak management, low facility quality, still-high maternal, infant and child mortality, poor infrastructure, shortage of trained personnel and unavailability of drugs; remedies include strengthening and expanding existing programs, family planning services at all levels, stronger reproductive health education, and expanded training of health personnel.

Transport sector policy. During the military government the sector was under strict state control through Proclamation No. 107/1976, which placed the entire commercial truck and passenger transport system under the government. The policy change of May 8, 1992 began the deregulation of freight transport, and Proclamation No. 14/1992 emphasized the promotion of efficiency and equitable distribution. After it, many private commercial freight and passenger operators left the corporation and formed independent associations, while some continued as associates of government enterprises. The new policy also allows free entry into existing associations and licenses to form new associations.

Tourism sector policy. Tourism should have been one of Ethiopia's largest industries given its many historical and natural sites and diverse cultural attractions, but the country has not realized the full economic benefits. In recent years, thanks to infrastructure such as roads and hotels and the government's marketing through embassies, tourism has grown significantly despite the world economic crisis, though much remains to be done. In 2009 the government launched a tourism development policy to increase tourist arrivals and optimize returns; its guiding principles are guiding the sector in a broad-based development framework, developing existing and new attractions and products, expanding vital infrastructure and tourist services, ensuring competitiveness in international tourism markets, and solving the serious capacity limitations. Because of too little attention and lack of finance, most issues in the policy document are still in implementation. The sector lacks coordination among stakeholders, attention to domestic tourism, awareness and incentives among local people, trained labor, infrastructure, quality service provision and promotion work. Improving transportation facilities, allocating an adequate budget, improving management, training manpower and promoting Ethiopia's tourism resources can address these challenges.

The Education Sector Review of the Imperial era, recommending universal primary education and ruralized curricula; it was not published until February 1974.
The Derg's development through cooperation campaign; about 60,000 students and teachers were deployed to rural areas in it.

workedExamples.problem: Classify the following service activities into one of the three activity types: training a mechanic's students at a college, repairing a taxi, and guiding visitors through a museum.
workedExamples.given: College training; car repair; museum guiding.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: services are physical, intellectual or aesthetic.
workedExamples.substitution: College training provides knowledge; car repair works with objects; museum guiding provides artistic experience.
workedExamples.calculation: Matching each service to its defining activity type: the college is intellectual, the repair is physical, and the museum is aesthetic.
workedExamples.answer: Intellectual: the college training; physical: taxi repair; aesthetic: museum guiding.

workedExamples.problem: The Derg deployed about 60,000 students and teachers from Haile Selassie I University and senior secondary schools to rural areas. If 40% of a pool of 150,000 students and teachers were deployed, was that consistent with the figure?
workedExamples.calculation: 40% of 150,000 equals the 60,000 deployment recorded in 1975.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, about 60,000 were deployed, matching the textbook figure for the Zemecha.

workedExamples.problem: A regional health bureau opens a health post in a village, trains its two workers, stocks essential drugs, and budgets it through block funding. Which goals of the 1993 health policy does this serve?
workedExamples.given: New health post; trained personnel; drug supply; block funding; district implementation.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: match actions to policy goals.
workedExamples.substitution: Decentralization to districts, accessible care for all segments, preventive and curative components, and human resource development.
workedExamples.calculation: Each action maps to a policy goal, jointly pushing toward cost-effective and efficient service delivery.
workedExamples.answer: It serves decentralization, accessibility for all segments, development of preventive and curative care, and human resource development.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia has rich tourism resources yet earns little from the sector. Using the textbook, rank three obstacles and one remedy for them.
workedExamples.given: Obstacles: poor coordination, untrained labor, weak promotion; remedy: government promotion through embassies.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: coordination and skills raise service quality and competitiveness.
workedExamples.substitution: Lack of coordination among stakeholders and shortage of trained labor directly limit service quality and promotion work.
workedExamples.calculation: Training manpower and promoting the country's resources, as the government does through embassies, raises arrivals and returns.
workedExamples.answer: Coordinate stakeholders and train workers while promoting tourism resources through embassies and infrastructure investment.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Imperial government had a published education policy, when the ESR only reached publication in February 1974.
Saying the Derg liberalized school ownership, when it nationalized all private schools in 1975.
Confusing ESDP with HSDP; ESDP covers education and HSDP covers health.
Assuming the health system became decentralized immediately after the 1978 primary health care declaration, when it remained highly centralized until the 1993 policy.
Attributing transport deregulation to Proclamation 107/1976, when that proclamation imposed state control and Proclamation 14/1992 liberalized.
Believing tourism fails only because of war and image, when coordination, trained labor, quality service and promotion are the listed obstacles.
Thinking all services are consumer-oriented, when some serve businesses or are mixed.
applications: Joining a parents and teachers association to improve facility quality in a rural school.
Understanding why a health extension worker in your kebele focuses on prevention, immunization and family planning.
Explaining how private transport associations formed after the 1992 deregulation organize bus routes in your town.
Estimating how a local historic site or festival could generate income if roads, hotels and promotion improved.
Keeping school textbooks and materials in good condition to ease the shortage problem your class faces today.
g11-economics-ue7-t3.summary: Service policies evolved by regime: education moved from the unpublished Imperial ESR through Derg nationalization and Zemecha to the six-component post-1991 ESDP, while health moved from the 1978 primary health care declaration to the 1993 Health Policy and the rolling 20-year HSDP with decentralization, prevention and private and NGO participation. Transport shifted from Proclamation 107/1976 state control to deregulation under Proclamation 14/1992, and tourism gained a development policy in 2009. All sub-sectors still face quality, access, staffing and finance constraints that remedies such as stakeholder participation, training, standards and budget allocation try to solve.
